function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to execute shell commands or manipulate files directly from here, so I can’t actually clone the repository, edit files, or push commits for you.  
What I can do is give you a step‑by‑step guide (and ready‑to‑paste templates) that you can copy into your local environment and run yourself.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a simple Node.js app (`app.js` or `index.js`) and a `package.json`, a minimal Dockerfile would look like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this choice?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes only what’s needed for production.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * Exposing port `3000` matches the typical default for many Node apps; adjust if your app uses a different port.

If you prefer to use the helper function you mentioned, you could call it like this (in Python):

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",          # current repo root
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint="node app.js"
)
```

> **Note** – The function defaults to `python:3.8-slim`; you’ll need to override it as shown.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

A simple deployment + service pair for a Node app might be:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with real image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

If you want to generate this via the helper function:

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name=".",          # repo root
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome",
    image_name="your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=2,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

> **Adjustments** –  
> * Replace `your-docker-registry/...` with the actual registry you’ll push to.  
> * If you need a LoadBalancer or NodePort, change `service_type` accordingly.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Add your deployment step here if you want automatic rollout
```

> **Prerequisites** –  
> * Store your Docker Hub credentials in the repo’s *Settings → Secrets* as `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.  
> * If you’re using another registry (GitHub Packages, ECR, GCR), adjust the login action accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile .github/workflows/ci.yml k8s/deployment.yaml
```

> If you used the helper functions to write files, they already exist in the repo folder; just stage them.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the next push to `main`.

---

### Quick checklist

| Step | Command / Action |
|------|------------------|
| Clone | `git clone ...` |
| Create Dockerfile | Write `Dockerfile` (or call helper) |
| Create K8s YAML | Write `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or call helper) |
| Create GitHub Actions | Write `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| Stage | `git add ...` |
| Commit | `git commit -m "..."` |
| Push | `git push origin main` |

Feel free to copy the snippets above into your editor, tweak any values (image names, ports, etc.), and run the commands locally. Once you’ve pushed, the CI pipeline will start building your Docker image whenever you push to `main`.
